Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service within AWS
and it uses machine learning, anomaly detection,
and threat intelligence to identify potential threats
in your AWS accounts and resources
such as S3 buckets, EC2 instances, EKS, et cetera.
So how does it do it?
It monitors various different log sources
such as VPC flow logs, DNS logs,
CloudTrail events, S3 data plane events,
and EKS control plane logs.
And then once it's ingest all these log source
it starts analyzing them.
Just to quickly touch upon
each of the different log sources,
so VPC flow logs is all your layer three traffic,
your 5-tuple.
So, source destination IP addresses,
port numbers, protocol,
whether that traffic was accepted or rejected.
All of that is logged in VPC Flow logs.
Your DNS logs are the DNS queries
that are made to the Amazon DNS servers
that are part of your AWS accounts.
You have the CloudTrail events
and CloudTrail is basically all the API calls
that are made to AWS, either through the AWS console,
SDKs, or the CLI,
and all of that is logged in in CloudTrail.
We also have the S3 data plane events
which is another version of CloudTrail
but specifically focusing on S3 object level events.
So think about your get objects,
put objects, delete objects
versus the bucket level events would be
get, create bucket, delete bucket, et cetera.
So that's the differentiation.
And then finally we have the EKS control plane logs
which is all the audit logs within the EKS service
where the user interacts with the EKS service
and the logs associated with that are also monitored.
One of the things to keep in mind
is when you do enable GuardDuty,
you don't have to enable these log sources separately.
They are all enabled by default by GuardDuty

they provide access to GuardDuty from the back lane.

Proofpoint and CrowdStrike.

As part of threat intelligence
